issues.legal_issue: A lender who is not a party to a mortgage deed may attest it when the deed is made in another person's name and the statutory attestation requirements are otherwise met.
material_facts: The borrower executed a mortgage deed in the name of another person for money advanced by the claimant.
The claimant, who was the actual lender but not a party to the deed, signed as one of the two attesting witnesses.
The deed had a second attesting witness.
issues.conclusion: The mortgage deed was validly attested; the actual lender was not disqualified from attesting because he was not a party to the deed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 59 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 require the specified witnessing for a mortgage deed but do not bar a person who is party to the transaction, yet not party to the deed, from attesting it. A party to the deed is disqualified because a party's testimony cannot replace the required examination of an attesting witness. The Court followed Balu Ravji Charat v. Gopal Gangadh Dhabu and Durga Din v. Suraj Bakhsh, and distinguished the principle associated with Seal v. Claridge and the Indian High Court decisions applying it to parties to deeds.

rule.if: attestation_validity_dispute and deed_requires_two_witnesses and actual_lender_attested and lender_not_deed_party and second_witness_qualified

predicates.attestation_validity_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an instrument requiring attestation was properly witnessed.
predicates.deed_requires_two_witnesses: The instrument was of a kind that required attestation by two witnesses.
predicates.actual_lender_attested: The person who advanced the money secured by the instrument signed it as an attesting witness.
predicates.lender_not_deed_party: The person who advanced the money was not a party to the instrument itself.
predicates.second_witness_qualified: A second witness met the applicable requirements for attesting the instrument.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns attestation of an instrument requiring two witnesses, an actual lender who attested it while not being a party to the instrument, together with a qualified second witness, means the mortgage deed is validly attested.

issues.legal_issue: The actual lender may sue to enforce a mortgage even when the mortgage deed is made in the name of a benamidar.
material_facts: The claimant advanced the money secured by the mortgage.
The mortgage deed was executed in the name of another person, who disputed the claimant's right to sue but did not prevail on that dispute.
The claimant sued to enforce the mortgage after the borrower failed to repay the loan.
issues.conclusion: The actual lender was entitled to sue upon the mortgage, although the deed was in the name of a benamidar.
issues.legal_principle: A person who provides the consideration for a transaction may maintain a suit concerning it; where the transaction is a mortgage, the actual lender may sue upon it. Section 84 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 recognizes benami transactions. Gur Narayan v. Sheo Lal Singh recognized that a benamidar may sue but did not hold that only the benamidar may sue; the beneficial owner is not thereby barred from enforcing the right. The Court also referred to Bilas Munwar v. Desraj Ranjit Singh in discussing the beneficial interest of the person who provides the purchase money.

rule.if: mortgage_enforcement_suit and claimant_provided_consideration and claimant_is_actual_lender and mortgage_deed_names_benamidar

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_suit: The proceeding is a suit to enforce a mortgage.
predicates.claimant_provided_consideration: The claimant provided the consideration for the transaction.
predicates.claimant_is_actual_lender: The claimant advanced the money secured by the mortgage.
predicates.mortgage_deed_names_benamidar: The mortgage deed names someone other than the person who provided the consideration.

issues.definition: When a suit seeks to enforce a mortgage, the claimant provided its consideration as the actual lender, and the deed names a benamidar, the actual lender may sue on the mortgage.
